newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - Politics to pose a problem.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - Politics to pose a problem.

text.p: Gilts will struggle to be a top performer in Europe this week as Britain's ruling Conservative Party holds its annual conference, which could highlight splits over economic policy and Europe. Add key inflation data on Thursday, with the underlying rate forecast to hold firm at 2.8 percent year-on-year for the fifth month in a row, and the result is a problematic recipe for the gilt market, analysts say.
So the past 10 days, during which the gilt/Bund spread has narrowed nearly 30 basis points, could soon be a distant memory.
The Conservative conference kicks off on Tuesday, after weekend press reports of right-wing Eurosceptics calling for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to be sacked.

But while many Conservatives are worried Clarke will not opt for aggressive income tax and interest rate cuts to boost flagging Conservative fortunes ahead of elections, that must be held by May 1997, the gilt market has the reverse worry.
"The market's concern may be that Mr Clarke will temper his anti-inflation stance...to turn away the wrath of party activists," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.
"This is probably to misread the Chancellor's temperament. All the same, he may not be willing to raise interest rates as some observers now assume."
Clarke delivers his keynote speech on Thursday, with Prime Minister John Major following on Friday.
Some economists had been calling for an early tightening of monetary policy, with evidence of a UK consumer boom mounting.
But figures released on Monday showed manufacturing output posted a surprise 0.3 percent fall in August, suggesting Clarke can comfortably resist an early rate rise.

"The figures offer confirmation that the gulf between consumers and industry remains wide," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets. "There is no chance that Mr Clarke will give in to Mr George's request for higher rates."

Minutes from the September 4 monetary meeting between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George will be released on Wednesday. Analysts said George is likely to have repeated his call for base rates to be raised from 5.75 percent to 6.00 but rates were in fact, left unchanged.
Fiscal and monetary policy are not the only areas of disagreement for the Conservatives during conference week. More damaging could be the split over a single European currency.

"The conference is likely to be dominated...by the question of the UK's relations with the EU," Lewis said. "The more Mr Major feels obliged to strike sceptical poses, the greater the residue of ill-will towards the UK is likely to be."

The big figure of the week is retail price inflation on Thursday. Economists forecast headline inflation will edge down to 2.0 percent year-on-year but that the underlying rate will again stick fast at 2.8 percent.

"High petrol prices, plus the echo of a drop in petrol prices a year ago, are likely to keep inflation stable or push it up slightly in September," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
He forecast a 2.9 percent underlying rate and said the effect of petrol prices could be even greater in October, pushing underlying inflation up to, or above, three percent.

All that means the gilt/Bund spread, in at 155 basis points from a peak of 183 two weeks ago, could slip a little. The December gilt future, which set a run of contract highs last week, peaking at 110-30, could have trouble revisiting highs.
If domestic problems were not enough, analysts said U.S. September producer price and retail sales figures, due on Friday, could also rock the boat.
Bond markets are still seeking to put into context the Federal Reserve's recent decision to leave U.S. interest rates on hold. Strong economic data will send T-bonds spinning lower.
